title: What are the KISS ("Keep It Simple, Stupid") and YAGNI ("You Aren't Gonna Need It") principles — KISS says prefer the simplest solution that works (avoid unnecessary abstraction, over-engineering, or clever code), YAGNI says don't build features or abstractions until they are actually needed (premature generalization wastes effort and adds complexity) — and how do you balance them against DRY (DRY can lead to premature abstraction if you extract a shared module for two things that only look similar today), and what are real examples of YAGNI violations (building a plugin architecture for a service that will only ever have one implementation, adding a message broker when direct REST calls suffice)?
shortTitle: KISS and YAGNI principles, balancing them against DRY, and real YAGNI violations

s1_definition.profdef: KISS, Keep It Simple Stupid, is a design principle that says the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem is usually the best one, because simple code is easier to read, test, debug, and change. YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, is a principle from extreme programming that says you should not build functionality or abstractions on speculation about future needs; build only what the current requirement demands. Both principles push back against over-engineering, and both must be balanced against DRY, which can tempt you into premature abstraction.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh needs a simple way to transfer money between two accounts. KISS says: write a straightforward transfer method that debits one account and credits another — do not build a configurable, plugin-based, rule-engine-driven transfer framework for a problem that is just "move money from A to B." YAGNI says: do not add support for fifteen currencies, scheduled transfers, and a message broker today just because someone imagines the bank might need them next year — add them when the bank actually asks. If you build the imaginary mansion before anyone needs the extra rooms, you waste effort and create corridors nobody walks down, which you still have to clean and maintain.
s1_definition.oneliner: KISS says prefer the simplest thing that works, YAGNI says do not build it until you actually need it, and both guard against over-engineering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** KISS, Keep It Simple Stupid, is a design principle that says the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem is usually the best one, because simple code is easier to read, test, debug, and change. YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, is a principle from extreme programming that says you should not build functionality or abstractions on speculation about future needs; build only what the current requirement demands. Both principles push back against over-engineering, and both must be balanced against DRY, which can tempt you into premature abstraction.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh needs a simple way to transfer money between two accounts. KISS says: write a straightforward transfer method that debits one account and credits another — do not build a configurable, plugin-based, rule-engine-driven transfer framework for a problem that is just "move money from A to B." YAGNI says: do not add support for fifteen currencies, scheduled transfers, and a message broker today just because someone imagines the bank might need them next year — add them when the bank actually asks. If you build the imaginary mansion before anyone needs the extra rooms, you waste effort and create corridors nobody walks down, which you still have to clean and maintain.

**One line to remember:** KISS says prefer the simplest thing that works, YAGNI says do not build it until you actually need it, and both guard against over-engineering.

sections.s2_technical:
**KISS** is about favouring clarity over cleverness. A violation is a dense one-liner using nested ternaries and stream tricks that nobody can read, where a plain if-else and a loop would be obvious. Another violation is introducing a design pattern, a framework, or a layer of indirection when a direct method call would do. The fix is always to ask "what is the simplest code that correctly solves exactly this problem?" Simple code has fewer places for bugs to hide and is cheaper to change when requirements shift. KISS does not mean naive or incorrect; it means not adding complexity that the problem does not require.

**YAGNI** is about resisting speculative generality. The temptation is to think "we might need to support multiple payment providers later, so let me build a pluggable provider framework now." YAGNI says do not, because you are guessing at a future that may never arrive, and meanwhile you pay for that guess immediately in extra code, extra abstractions, and extra maintenance. The future requirement, when it actually appears, is usually different from what you imagined anyway, so the speculative structure often has to be torn out and rebuilt. The discipline is to build for today's requirement, keep the code clean enough to change, and add the generalisation when the second real case actually shows up.

Now the crucial balancing act with **DRY**. DRY tells you to remove duplication, but applied too eagerly it directly conflicts with KISS and YAGNI, because it tempts you into premature abstraction. The classic trap is seeing two code blocks that look similar today and extracting them into one shared module or base class. If those two blocks represent different business rules that merely coincide right now, you have created an abstraction that will fight you the moment they diverge — you will start adding boolean flags and conditionals to the shared code to serve both masters, and that shared code becomes a tangled mess that is harder to understand than the original duplication. This is why the rule of thumb "duplicate until it hurts, then abstract" exists, often phrased as the rule of three: wait until you have three genuine repetitions that truly change together before unifying them. DRY is about a single source of truth for one piece of knowledge, not about deleting every line that looks alike.

So how do you balance all three in practice? You let KISS and YAGNI be the default stance: build the simplest thing that meets the current requirement, do not add abstractions on speculation. You apply DRY only when you have real, repeated knowledge that genuinely changes together, not coincidental similarity. When you are unsure whether two similar things are really the same rule, you keep them separate — accepting a little duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction, and it is far easier to later merge two things than to untangle a bad shared abstraction. Essentially, DRY removes duplication of knowledge; KISS and YAGNI stop you from inventing structure before the knowledge is actually shared.

Real **YAGNI violations** are worth naming because interviewers ask for them. Building a plugin architecture with interfaces, a registry, and dynamic loading for a service that will only ever have a single implementation is a classic violation — you pay for extensibility you never use. Adding a message broker like Kafka when a simple direct REST call between two services would comfortably handle the load is another; you have introduced an entire piece of infrastructure, with its operational burden, retries, and monitoring, to solve a problem you do not have yet. Other examples include writing a generic configurable rules engine when there are only three fixed rules, adding caching layers before you have measured any performance problem, designing a database schema with dozens of "future-proof" nullable columns nobody populates, and creating abstract base classes with a single subclass "in case we need more." Each one trades real, immediate complexity for a speculative benefit that usually never materialises.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs a fee calculator. There is exactly one fee rule today: a flat transfer fee. A well-meaning engineer proposed building a configurable rules engine with pluggable fee strategies, a rules-loading mechanism, and a message broker to publish fee events "for the future." That is a YAGNI violation — it adds huge complexity for a single, simple rule. The KISS and YAGNI approach is to write a plain fee calculation now and only generalise if and when a second real fee type appears.

Problem 2 — We want to show the contrast concretely: the over-engineered design versus the simple design, and then show that when a genuine second requirement arrives (a percentage-based fee for large transfers), extending the simple design is cheap and does not require the speculative machinery we avoided earlier.

In the mini-project we will implement the simple, KISS-and-YAGNI-honouring `FeeCalculator` that handles today's flat fee directly. We will compute the fee for Rajesh's transfer. Then, when a real second requirement appears, we will show that adding a percentage fee for large amounts is a small, clear change — demonstrating that starting simple did not paint us into a corner. We will also include a short comment block describing what the over-engineered version would have looked like, so the reader sees what we deliberately did not build.

The code contains: a simple `FeeCalculator` with a direct method; a small extension when a real second rule arrives; and a `main` that calculates fees for a normal transfer and a large transfer.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a small transfer of forty thousand rupees and a large transfer of twelve lakh rupees.

Step 1: The `FeeCalculator` is created with no dependencies — no rules engine, no registry, no message broker. It holds three plain constants: the flat fee, the large-transfer threshold, and the large-transfer rate. This is the KISS and YAGNI choice.

Step 2: `computeFee` is called with the forty thousand transfer. The amount is compared with the large threshold of ten lakh using `compareTo`. Forty thousand is below the threshold, so the flat fee of twenty-five rupees is returned directly.

Step 3: `computeFee` is called with the twelve lakh transfer. Twelve lakh is above the ten lakh threshold, so the percentage branch runs: twelve lakh times 0.05 percent, rounded with `BigDecimal` to two decimals, giving six hundred rupees.

Step 4: Notice what did not happen. There was no strategy lookup, no plugin loading, no event published to a broker. The second real rule was handled by adding one small branch, which shows that starting simple left the code easy to extend rather than trapped.

```
2026-10-26 10:10:00 [INFO] === KISS/YAGNI: simplest fee that meets today's need ===
2026-10-26 10:10:00 [INFO] Fee for Rs.40000 = Rs.25.00
2026-10-26 10:10:00 [INFO] === Real second rule appears — extend simply ===
2026-10-26 10:10:00 [INFO] Fee for Rs.1200000 = Rs.600.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
KISS and YAGNI are two principles that both push back against over-engineering. KISS, Keep It Simple Stupid, says the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem is usually the best, because simple code is easier to read, test, debug, and change. YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, says do not build features or abstractions on speculation about future needs — build only what today's requirement demands, because the imagined future rarely arrives as imagined, and meanwhile you pay for the guess in immediate complexity.

In my banking project a colleague wanted to build a configurable rules engine with pluggable fee strategies and a Kafka topic to publish fee events, even though we had exactly one fee rule at the time. That was a clear YAGNI violation — enormous machinery for a single flat fee. Following KISS and YAGNI, I wrote a plain fee method with a couple of constants. Later, when a genuine second rule actually arrived — a percentage fee for large transfers — extending the simple design was a tiny, obvious change, which proved that starting simple had not trapped us; it had kept the code cheap to change.

The balancing act I always explain is against DRY. DRY is right that each piece of knowledge should have one home, but applied too eagerly it tempts you into premature abstraction, which fights KISS and YAGNI. The classic trap is seeing two blocks that merely look alike today and extracting them into one shared abstraction. If those blocks represent different rules that only coincide for now, the shared code becomes a mess of flags the moment they diverge. So I let KISS and YAGNI be the default — simplest thing for today — and I apply DRY only when the same knowledge genuinely repeats and changes together, often waiting for the rule of three. My guiding phrase is that duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction, because merging two things later is easy, while untangling a bad shared abstraction is painful.

Real YAGNI violations I have seen and avoided include building a plugin architecture for a service with only one implementation, adding a message broker when a direct REST call comfortably handles the load, writing a generic configurable rules engine for three fixed rules, and adding caching before measuring any performance problem. Each trades certain, immediate complexity for a speculative benefit that usually never materialises, so I resist them until a real requirement forces the issue.
---

keyPoints: DRY: Do not Repeat Yourself — extract common logic
KISS: Keep It Simple — simplest solution that works
YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It — do not build for imagined futures
Balance: DRY vs readability, YAGNI vs preparedness
